This initial mass of about 6 grams contrasts sharply with the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults, which reaches about 82.7 grams [Wwi = about 82.7 grams] under favorable conditions. Body length measurements from field studies indicate that adults attain a typical snout-to-vent length of approximately 13 centimeters [Li = approximately 13 centimeters], though individuals may range between 12 and 14 centimeters depending on geographic provenance and local resource availability. This substantial size increase is supported by a diet rich in arthropods and fruit, which provides the necessary protein and energy for rapid tissue accretion during the austral summer.

At a thermoneutral temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], respirometry trials revealed that Gray mouse lemurs exhibit a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 82.7 milliliters per hour [JOi = 82.7 milliliters per hour]. This elevated metabolic rate, recorded at a temperature approaching the upper critical limit of the species' thermoneutral zone, is among the highest reported for any cheirogaleid and likely reflects the energetic demands of maintaining a high body temperature in a small-bodied endotherm. The rate of 82.7 milliliters per hour underscores the substantial metabolic cost of thermoregulation in an animal that frequently enters daily torpor to conserve energy. Comparative data suggest that the basal metabolism of Microcebus murinus is more than double that of larger-bodied lemurids per unit of body mass, a pattern consistent with the general allometric scaling of metabolic rates across mammals.

Parturition typically coincides with the onset of the rainy season, ensuring that peak lactation demand aligns with maximal arthropod abundance.

The developmental timeline from birth to nutritional independence in Gray mouse lemurs follows a predictable sequence under thermoneutral conditions.
